newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Police yield to street party, EU warns Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Police yield to street party, EU warns Milosevic.

text.p: Serbian opposition demonstrators revelled in the streets of Belgrade on Friday after riot police abandoned their cordons, and the EU warned President Slobodan Milosevic to embrace democracy or languish in isolation.
Thousands ran with abandon through the streets of Belgrade before dawn after students persuaded police to dismantle their cordons.

The students outlasted police in a 12-hour standoff on the 53rd consecutive day of mass demonstrations throughout Serbia against the Milosevic government's annulment of municipal election victories by the Zajedno (Together) coalition.

Students had vowed to stand in front of police lines until they were allowed to march. After the police lines dissolved, demonstrators roamed city boulevards, singing and dancing despite the overnight mid-winter cold.
"This is a great thing happening tonight. It's our chance to change the future and we'll do it," said one woman.
Milosevic on Wednesday conceded the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition had won in Serbia's second city Nis, one of 14 municipalities including the capital Belgrade in dispute.

But Zajedno leaders vowed protests would continue until all their claims were met. They urged Belgraders to drive en masse into the city centre at 2 p.m. (1300 gmt) on Friday to create a "traffic collapse", as they did last Sunday.

In a statement released on Thursday night, the EU urged Milosevic to accept all of Zajedno's poll victories as verified by a factfinding delegation of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe that visited Belgrade last month.

"The Union... calls on the authorities...and in particular President Milosevic to fully accept the conclusions and recommendations (of the OSCE report) and act on them without delay," the statement said.

"Only reform directed towards full democratisation and liberalisation of the political and economic system, in dialogue with the opposition, as well as respect for human rights ... will allow for the full integration of Yugoslavia into the international community."

Federal Yugoslavia, which comprises only Serbia and tiny Montenegro, has been isolated internationally since 1992 when diplomatic and economic sanctions were imposed to punish Serbia for fomenting the war in Bosnia.
The United Nations rescinded most of the sanctions in late 1995 after Milosevic persuaded the Bosnian Serbs, his former nationalist proxies in Bosnia, to sign the Dayton peace treaty.
But an "outer wall" of sanctions left in place by Western governments has prevented a full resumption of political and commercial relations with Yugoslavia.

Belgrade has still not been readmitted to the United Nations or key financial institutions like the World Bank, blocking major credits and investment desperately needed by Yugoslavia to rebuild its wrecked economy.

The Serbian government banned protest marches after clashes between pro and anti-government demonstrators on December 24. But the edict, only intermittently enforced on some days and rigorously on others, fell apart on Thursday night.
After hours of cat-and-mouse games with whistle-blowing students, police apparently got orders to retreat and demonstrators were free to roam Belgrade's streets.

Important players in the Yugoslav power structure have parted ways with Milosevic over the election fiasco, including army officers and Orthodox churchmen who have called for the popular will to be honoured according to the constitution.

They were joined on Friday by the normally staunchly pro-Milosevic Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences. The academicians called for police to leave the streets and reinstatement of the election outcome.
"By persisting in the defence of untenable positions and ignoring the conclusions of the OSCE..., the regime is provoking threats of new sanctions," they said in a letter.
The United States said on Thursday Milosevic's recognition of Zajedno's victory in Nis did not go far enough and he could not win world applause by "dribbling out minor concessions".

U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum began a trip to The Hague, Brussels, Sarajevo and Zagreb to discuss issues pertaining to former Yugoslavia including Bosnia's postwar reconstruction and the political crisis in Serbia.
His itinerary deliberately excluded Belgrade.

Paul Poudade, a senior French foreign ministry official, was in Belgrade to urge Milosevic to heed the OSCE. Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos was due on Sunday to try to ease tensions between Milosevic and the opposition parties.
